# Devlore

*Every repo has its lore.*

Devlore watches your GitHub repos and keeps their documentation honest — without anyone having to write it by hand. Push code, and Devlore drafts what changed and why. Cut a release, and it folds those drafts into real, reviewed reference docs — drafted automatically, still reviewed by a human before anything becomes official. Once your history is caught up, just ask it questions: why did we switch to Postgres in March, what does this repo actually do, why did we choose this approach over that one.

It's especially useful if you're building with AI. Your product doc stays live and current, which makes it exactly the kind of grounded, up-to-date context an AI coding agent actually needs — closer to a running source of truth than a doc you wrote once and forgot. And when AI lets a codebase move fast, it's easy to lose track of every decision, every idea you meant to come back to, every "fix this later" — Devlore keeps that trail intact automatically, so your memory doesn't fall behind your pace.

It runs entirely on your own machine, using your own Claude API key — your code and your questions never pass through a server Devlore operates. Link a repo, and Devlore starts keeping its story straight.

## What's new in v0.1.7

There's nothing user-facing to report for this release. The one change — a generated onboarding guide added to devlore's own repository to help new contributors get oriented — is internal documentation for people working on devlore's codebase, not a feature or change that affects how you use devlore.

## Install and run

```bash
npx @starterculture/devlore
```

That starts the local server at `http://localhost:4173` and serves the chat UI in your browser — no config files, no environment variables to set up first. (You can also `npm install -g @starterculture/devlore` and run `devlore` if you'd rather not re-fetch it via `npx` every time.)

## First run

You'll need three credentials over the course of setup — each one is pasted directly into the browser, once, and stored from there in your OS's own credential store (Keychain / Credential Manager / Secret Service). None of them ever go into a config file.

1. **Anthropic API key.** The first time you open the page, a setup panel prompts for it.
   - Get one at [console.anthropic.com/settings/keys](https://console.anthropic.com/settings/keys) — no special scope, just create a key and copy it.
   - Paste it into the setup panel. It's validated with a cheap test call before being stored, so a typo is caught immediately.

2. **GitHub token for linking or creating a project.** Open "Link a project" in the left rail — the wizard prompts for this one.
   - Create a **fine-grained personal access token** at [github.com/settings/personal-access-tokens/new](https://github.com/settings/personal-access-tokens/new).
   - Repository access: **All repositories**.
   - Permissions: **Actions** (Read and write), **Contents** (Read and write), **Secrets** (Read and write), **Workflows** (Read and write), **Administration** (Read and write — needed to create a new repo).
   - Paste it into the wizard. It's used to write workflow files and secrets into the repos you link. If you're the first person to link a project on this GitHub account, it also creates your private `devlore-vault` documentation repo the first time — but if you're joining a project a teammate already set up, Devlore detects and reuses their existing vault automatically instead, no extra steps needed.

3. **GitHub vault read token.** Once step 2 has resolved a vault for you — created, reused from your own account, or adopted from a project you just joined — a third field unlocks in the setup panel, pre-filled with the exact repo it needs.
   - Create another fine-grained token at the same URL, this time scoped to **only that one vault repo**, with **Contents: Read-only**.
   - This is what the local server uses to pull your documentation into the chat UI — deliberately narrower than the token in step 2, since it never needs to write anything.

Once a project is linked (step 2), push some commits and Devlore starts drafting log entries automatically. Open the chat and ask it anything about the project — it answers from the same docs it's keeping current.

The fastest way to understand everything the app can do is its own in-app **User Manual** — click "User Manual" in the left rail. It's generated by Devlore itself and covers every feature end to end.

## About the paid tier

A subscription is meant to unlock a few extra features (a visualizer, QA test plans, release notes, and an onboarding guide for new contributors) on top of the free chat/log/consolidation core. **In this beta, that's a placeholder, not a real payment flow yet** — a dev-only "Unlock features" toggle in the left rail flips those tabs open for testing. No real subscription exists to buy. Everything else described above works for real today.

## Questions or issues

If something doesn't behave the way the User Manual says it should, that's a bug worth reporting back to whoever gave you access to this beta.
